title: Warmer local winters were followed by about 0.8% more resident birds per degree C and no change in migratory birds on 4,068 North American survey routes in 1970-2024
abstract: Question: does local winter cold change the next breeding-season counts of resident birds, with migratory birds as a negative control? Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey 2025 release (6,870,825 route-species-year records, 368 species, 4,068 routes, 1970-2024), NOAA GHCN_CAMS monthly temperature, and the AVONET migration class (95 resident, 74 partial, 199 migratory species). Method: log(count+1) with species x route x observer and species x year fixed effects; December-February temperature anomaly from a route trend, with class-specific slopes; controls for spring and summer anomalies, survey weather, date and first observer year; two-way clustered intervals (space and year); plan written before model fits. Results: a winter 1 C warmer than the trend was followed by +0.81% (95% CI +0.48 to +1.15) resident counts, +0.55% (+0.26 to +0.85) partial-migrant counts and -0.00% (-0.23 to +0.23) migrant counts. The resident slope was positive with an interval above zero in East and West, 1970-1996 and 1997-2024. A year-relabel permutation test gave p = 0.002 for residents and p = 0.92 for migrants. An extreme cold winter (lowest 10%) gave -2.0% (-3.1 to -1.0) for residents and 0.0% for migrants. The resident slope was larger in the cold part of the species winter range (-0.24 per SD, -0.43 to -0.05). 74 of 95 resident species had positive slopes; Carolina Wren had the largest. Limitations: counts are an index without a detection model; seasonal mean temperature does not measure snow or short cold spells; AVONET gives one class per species; the next-winter placebo for residents was -0.26 (-0.57 to +0.04); migrants had a small positive slope in 1970-1996; the design is correlational. One SD of winter anomaly (1.7 C) changes resident counts by only about 1.4%.
